warmup.q: A query reads 4 Parquet files, keeps the captured payments, adds up the amounts for each shop, and asks for the result with collect(). Spark gives each file its own piece of work, and it's set to split the grouped data into 4 pieces too (spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 4). A feature that can change these numbers while the job runs is turned off. How many tasks, single pieces of work, run in total?
warmup.why: Adding up per shop needs every payment of a shop in one place, so Spark has to move rows between the pieces of work. That step is called a shuffle, and it splits the job into two stages. Stage 1 runs one task per file (4) to read, filter and add up what each file holds. Stage 2 runs one task per piece of the grouped data (4) for the final sums. 4 + 4 = 8. 200 is Spark's default number of pieces after a shuffle, but this query set it to 4. The third section builds this count step by step.

sections.h: Spark writes down every step and runs nothing until an action
sections.html:
Here's the nightly report from the opening, written with Spark's DataFrame API, the set of functions your code calls:

val totals = spark.read().parquet("build/l05/payments")      // 400,000 payments, 4 files
    .where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED"))
    .withColumn("amount_eur", col("amount_cents").divide(100))
    .groupBy("merchant_id")
    .agg(sum("amount_eur").alias("total_eur"))
totals.collectAsList()

A DataFrame is Spark's table: named, typed columns, with the rows split into partitions, slices of the data that different machines can work on at the same time. Read the code from the top. It reads 400,000 payments from 4 Parquet files and keeps the captured ones, the payments where the money really moved. It works out each amount in euros and adds up the euros for each shop. The last line asks for the result as a list. (Spark 4.3.0, from October 2026, is the newest release. The labs pin 4.1.4, because Iceberg, the table format of lesson 11, supports Spark only up to 4.1. Spark runs a query the same way in both.)

Think about how a system could run this. Version 1: eagerly, one step at a time. A Kotlin List works this way: payments.filter { }.map { } runs each step at once and builds a complete new list before the next step starts. On a 1 TB table (a terabyte, a million million bytes), the where would write out every captured payment before withColumn could begin. And the where can't know that later steps use only two of the columns, so it carries all of them along.

Version 2: lazily. A Kotlin Sequence or a Java stream only records what to do, until a last step asks for a result. Spark works this way. where, select, withColumn, groupBy and join are transformations: each one returns a new DataFrame that describes a computation, and runs nothing. collect, count, show and write are actions: they need an answer, so they make Spark do the work. In the words of Spark's own guide, transformations "do not compute their results right away". That's the waiter writing the order down.

Waiting pays off at the action, because Spark then sees the whole query at once, like the head chef reading the whole order. Spark's optimizer, the part that rewrites a query into a faster one with the same answer, is called Catalyst. It takes the query through four forms, and explain("extended") prints all of them:

  1. Parsed: your steps as written.
  2. Analyzed: column names and types checked against the schema, the list of columns and their types. Spark does this as you build, so a typo in a column name fails on the where line.
  3. Optimized: rewritten. Here the optimizer drops payment_id, which nothing uses.
  4. Physical: the operators, the small building blocks that will really run. The line that reads the files shows PushedFilters and a three-column ReadSchema: the filter handed to the Parquet reader and the column pruning from Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown.

Laziness has a cost too. Every action runs the whole plan again, from the files. A line like log.info("rows: ${df.count()}") before df.write() looks like a harmless log message. It's a second full run: Spark reads and filters the input once for the count and again for the write, so a two-hour job quietly takes four. Keep one action at the end. When you really mean to reuse a result, cache() keeps it; the lesson The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching shows how.

A DataFrame holds a plan, not rows. Count your actions.

The Try it shows how much of the time the action takes. Next, we'll see where that work runs.

sections.h: One driver plans, and executors run one task per partition, in waves
sections.html:
collect() started real work. Where does that work run?

Back in the restaurant, the head chef reads the orders, writes the plan and cooks nothing. The line cooks each work on one ticket at a time, and when there are more tickets than cooks, the tickets wait their turn. A Spark program is built the same way, from two kinds of process, a process being one running program.

The driver is the head chef. It's the JVM, the program that runs Java and Kotlin code, that runs your main(). It holds the SparkSession, the object your code talks to, builds and optimizes plans, and hands out work. The executors are the cooks. They're JVMs on the worker machines of a cluster, a group of machines that work on one job together, and they do the work. Each executor has some number of cores, the parts of a processor that each run one thing at a time. Each core is a slot that runs one task at a time. Spark's cluster overview says the same in its own words. Executors run tasks in several threads, and stay up for the whole application. (A thread is a path of work inside one program; several can run at the same time.)

A task is the unit of work, one ticket: one partition of the data pushed through a chain of steps. For files, a partition is at most 128 MB of a file (spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes), and Spark packs small files together. HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived cut its input into splits the same way. So the data decides how many tasks there are, and the cluster decides how many slots run them. When there are more tasks than slots, the tasks run in waves.

Put numbers on it. 8 tasks on 2 slots run as 4 waves of 2. If each task takes 300 ms, the stage takes about 1.2 seconds. Double the slots, and it takes about 0.6 seconds. A stage of 200 tasks on 12 cores runs as 17 waves, and the last wave is only 8 tasks wide, so 4 cores sit idle at the end.

Two rules fall out of this. Fewer partitions than slots wastes cores: a table in 4 partitions on a 64-core cluster uses 4 of them. And one partition much bigger than the others makes one long task that the whole stage waits for, the straggler of HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived. Spark's tuning guide suggests 2 to 3 tasks per core, which keeps every slot busy and keeps the last wave short.

On a laptop, local[2] puts the driver and one executor in your own JVM, and the executor gets 2 slots, which are threads. local[*] gives it one slot per core. The scheduler, the part of the driver that hands tasks to free slots, is the same one a cluster uses, only with no network between the parts.

So far, every task has worked on its own partition, like a cook with one ticket. Next, we'll meet a step that needs something from every cook at once.

try.title: Watch tasks run in waves
steps: From the labs folder, run SlotsDemo. It runs one stage of 8 tasks that each work for 300 ms, first with local[2], then with local[4].
Predict both total times before you look.
Set tasks = 9 at the top of main, and predict the waves for local[4] before you run it again.

code.title: SlotsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l06.demo import org.apache.spark.TaskContext import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.MapPartitionsFunction import org.apache.spark.sql.Encoders /** * Runs one stage of 8 tasks, each of which works for 300 ms, first with 2 task slots and then * with 4. Every task reports its partition and when it started; tasks that started together are * one wave. */ fun main() { val tasks = 8 // try 9 for (slots in listOf(2, 4)) { val spark = demoSpark("local[$slots]") val task = MapPartitionsFunction<Long, String> { _ -> val start = System.currentTimeMillis() Thread.sleep(300) // pretend to read and filter 300 ms of data listOf("${TaskContext.getPartitionId()} $start").iterator() } spark.range(0, tasks.toLong(), 1, tasks).mapPartitions(task, Encoders.STRING()).collectAsList() // warm-up: the first job pays for class loading val t0 = System.nanoTime() val started = spark.range(0, tasks.toLong(), 1, tasks).mapPartitions(task, Encoders.STRING()).collectAsList() .map { it.split(" ").let { (p, t) -> p.toInt() to t.toLong() } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("local[$slots]: $tasks tasks of 300 ms each took $ms ms") val first = started.minOf { it.second } // tasks that started within 100 ms of each other ran side by side: one wave val waves = started.sortedBy { it.second }.fold(mutableListOf<MutableList<Pair<Int, Long>>>()) { acc, t -> if (acc.isEmpty() || t.second - acc.last().first().second > 100) acc += mutableListOf(t) else acc.last() += t acc } waves.forEachIndexed { i, w -> println(" wave %d starts at %4d ms: partitions %s".format(i + 1, w.first().second - first, w.map { it.first }.sorted().joinToString(", "))) } spark.stop() } }

sections.h: Where a job splits into stages: the shuffle
sections.html:
Not every step can run inside one task. Look at the report's two halves.

where and withColumn are narrow steps: each output partition needs exactly one input partition. Task 2 can filter file 2 without looking at anything else. So Spark chains narrow steps inside one task. It reads a batch of rows, filters it, works out the euros and adds them to a running sum per shop. Then it moves on to the next batch, with no in-between result written anywhere. In the physical plan, *(1) in front of several operators means Spark compiled them together into one generated function. Spark calls this whole-stage code generation.

groupBy is wide: the total for shop 42 needs rows from every input partition. In the kitchen, that's plating a meal. The steak from the grill and the fries from the fryer must meet at the pass, the counter where each order's dishes come together, before anything goes out. The lesson HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived showed how to do this across machines. Each task splits its output into one part for each task of the next step. It picks the part by hashing the key: turning the shop number into a number and taking the remainder. It writes the parts to its own machine's disk. Then each task of the next step fetches its part from every earlier task. That's the shuffle, and a Spark plan calls it Exchange. No task after the shuffle can start until every task before it has finished writing, so the shuffle cuts the work in two.

Now three words fit together. A job is everything one action runs. A stage is a stretch of narrow steps between shuffles. It runs as one task per partition, every task doing the same steps on a different partition. A task is one partition going through one stage. For a plan that reads one input:

stages = number of Exchanges + 1
tasks  = input partitions + the partitions of each shuffle

The report has one Exchange, so two stages. Stage 1 has a task per input partition: 4 files, 4 tasks. Stage 2 has a task per shuffle partition, set by spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: 200 by default, 4 in these demos. One job, two stages, eight tasks. The stepper below walks through it. Spark draws a job's stages, and the arrows between them, as a graph called the DAG (directed acyclic graph: arrows that only go forward, never round in a loop).

A shuffle ends a stage. Count the Exchange nodes and add one.

One feature changes the count. Since Spark 3.2, adaptive query execution (AQE) is on by default. It runs every stage that ends in a shuffle as a job of its own, looks at how big the shuffle's output really was, and plans the rest again. In the Try it, AQE sees four tiny shuffle partitions and merges them into one: 2 jobs and 5 tasks for the same report. The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching covers AQE, and this lesson's tests turn it off to see the plain model.

The Spark UI, the web page a Spark program serves while it runs, shows the same picture. Its Jobs tab lists the jobs. A job's page draws its stages as the DAG, and a stage's page lists every task with its time and its shuffle bytes.

The shuffle files sit on one machine's disk, in one copy. That raises an awkward question: what happens when that machine dies? Next, we'll find out.

try.title: Count the stages, then open the UI
steps: From the labs folder, run StagesDemo. It prints the report's physical plan, then what the scheduler ran with AQE off and with AQE on.
Count the Exchange nodes, and predict the stages and tasks for the run with AQE off before you read that line.

sections.h: A failed task is run again from its recipe: lineage
sections.html:
Machines die in the middle of jobs. In HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived, MapReduce lived with that by writing every job's output to HDFS three times, on three machines. That made long chains of jobs slow. Spark keeps the data between steps in memory and on local disk, in one copy. So how does it get a lost partition back?

It cooks the dish again. In the kitchen, when a cook drops a plate, the chef doesn't restart the whole order; the cook makes that one dish again from the recipe. Under every DataFrame plan sits a chain of RDDs (resilient distributed datasets, Spark's original way of describing data spread over machines). Each RDD knows its parent and the function that turns a parent partition into one of its own. That chain of parents is the lineage, the recipe. When the task for partition 2 fails, Spark doesn't restore anything from a copy. It looks up how partition 2 was made and runs exactly that again: read file 2, filter, add up. No other partition is touched.

This works only because tasks are deterministic: run one twice on the same input, and you get the same output. MapReduce needed the same rule to re-run its map tasks. And here the kitchen picture breaks. A remade dish uses fresh ingredients and comes out a little different, while a Spark retry reads the same input and must produce exactly the same rows.

toDebugString() prints the lineage of an RDD. In the Try it, the lineage reads, from the bottom: parallelize, map, mapToPair, then reduceByKey. The indented +- before the top line marks the shuffle, so the lineage also shows where the stages split.

The scheduler gives each task up to 4 attempts by default (spark.task.maxFailures). The failure that costs most is a dead executor whose stage 1 tasks had already finished. Their shuffle files were on its disk, so they're gone. The stage 2 tasks fail to fetch them, and Spark re-runs only those stage 1 tasks, from lineage, before stage 2 tries again. The other way round is cheap. When a stage 2 task fails, its retry fetches the shuffle files again and reads none of the input. Shuffle files are where recomputing stops.

Slow tasks get another MapReduce fix, the backup task, under the name speculative execution. When a task runs far longer than the median task of its stage (the middle one, when the times are lined up), Spark starts a second copy of it. It keeps whichever copy finishes first. It's still off by default in Spark 4.3 (spark.speculation=false). A duplicate is harmless only when the task's output counts once, and a task that writes rows into a database or calls another company's service would do it twice.

You'll still meet RDDs in the UI, in lineage and in old code. The difference matters. An RDD holds plain objects and runs your lambdas, small functions written inline such as { i -> i % 5 }, and Spark can't see inside a lambda. So it can't push a filter into Parquet or drop unused columns. A DataFrame is made of column expressions that Catalyst understands, and Spark turns it into RDDs only at the very end.

Spark can optimize only what it can read. Write DataFrames.

One caution for laptops: plain local[2] gives each task a single attempt, so one failure fails the whole job. The demo uses local[2,4]: 2 slots, and up to 4 attempts per task, like a cluster.

Recomputing makes one failure cheap. A shuffle stays expensive, though: every row it moves is written to disk and fetched again, and the next lesson opens it up.

try.title: Crash one task on purpose
steps: From the labs folder, run RetryDemo. It prints an RDD's lineage, then runs it with partition 2 set to crash on its first attempt.
Before you run it: how many tasks will run in total, and will the result be right?
Change the master, the local[...] setting at the top, to local[2], with no retries, and run it again. What happens to the job?

code.title: RetryDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l06.demo import org.apache.logging.log4j.Level import org.apache.logging.log4j.core.config.Configurator import org.apache.spark.TaskContext import org.apache.spark.api.java.JavaSparkContext import org.apache.spark.scheduler.SparkListener import org.apache.spark.scheduler.SparkListenerTaskEnd import scala.Tuple2 /** * Shows an RDD's lineage, then makes one task fail on its first attempt and watches Spark run that * task again from the same lineage. `local[2,4]` means 2 slots and up to 4 attempts per task. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark("local[2,4]") Configurator.setLevel("org.apache.spark.executor.Executor", Level.OFF) // no stack trace for the planned crash val sc = JavaSparkContext(spark.sparkContext()) spark.sparkContext().addSparkListener(object : SparkListener() { override fun onTaskEnd(taskEnd: SparkListenerTaskEnd) { val info = taskEnd.taskInfo() println(" stage %d, partition %d, attempt %d: %s".format( taskEnd.stageId(), info.index(), info.attemptNumber(), if (info.successful()) "ok" else "FAILED (${taskEnd.reason().javaClass.simpleName})")) } }) // per merchant: how many payments, from 4 partitions of made-up (merchant, amount) pairs val counts = sc.parallelize((0 until 40_000).toList(), 4) .map { i -> // partition 2 crashes the first time it runs, like a machine that dies mid-task if (TaskContext.getPartitionId() == 2 && TaskContext.get().attemptNumber() == 0) error("executor lost") i % 5 } .mapToPair { m -> Tuple2(m, 1) } .reduceByKey { a, b -> a + b } println("lineage:") println(counts.toDebugString().lines().joinToString("\n") { " " + it.replace(Regex(""" at \w+\.kt:\d+ \[]"""), "") }) println("running:") val result = counts.collectAsMap().toSortedMap() spark.sparkContext().listenerBus().waitUntilEmpty() println("result: $result") spark.stop() }

running:
  stage 0, partition 1, attempt 0: ok
  stage 0, partition 0, attempt 0: ok
  stage 0, partition 2, attempt 0: FAILED (ExceptionFailure)

The (4) is the number of partitions of each RDD. Only partition 2 of stage 0 ran twice; the other seven tasks ran once. (Spark counts stages from 0, so its stage 0 is our stage 1.) The second attempt recomputed partition 2 from its lineage, starting at parallelize, and the result is exact: 40,000 values, 8,000 for each of the 5 keys. The order of the ok lines changes from run to run, because tasks finish in whatever order the threads get to them. With plain local[2], the first failure ends everything: Spark logs Task 2 in stage 0.0 failed 1 times; aborting job, and collect throws a SparkException.

aside.title: If Spark can recompute anything, why keep shuffle files at all?
aside.html: Because a partition after a shuffle depends on every partition before it. Shop 42's total was built from pieces of all four files. Without the shuffle files, a lost stage 2 task would mean re-running all four stage 1 tasks. On a 1 TB job, with one task per 128 MB piece, that's all 7,451 of them. Keeping the files on disk turns that into one fetch. The paper that introduced RDDs makes the same point: losing data behind a wide step can force a lot of recomputation.

opening:
Picture ordering dinner for eight at a busy restaurant. The waiter writes each dish down as you say it, and nothing is cooked yet. Work starts when the order reaches the kitchen, and the head chef reads all of it before anyone cooks.

Spark, a program that runs data jobs across many machines, treats your code the same way. A teammate times each line of a nightly report: reading the files, 52 ms; filtering, 40 ms; grouping by shop, 80 ms. The last line, collect(), takes a second on a laptop and forty minutes on the real data.

It's easy to read Spark code like ordinary Kotlin, where each line runs when you reach it. A Spark line only adds a dish to the order.

In Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown, we watched what Spark read from a file. In this lesson, we'll build that report line by line, watch work run in waves, find where a job splits, and crash part of it on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a report whose lines each took milliseconds, until the last one took all the time. Every line before collect() only wrote a dish down. The action cooked the order: one job of two stages and eight tasks, split at the one shuffle.

Find some Spark code, your own or an example from Spark's documentation, and look for count(), show() or collect() before the final write(). Each one is a full extra run of everything above it.

Next, we'll open the shuffle itself, and find out what it writes, why many small pieces make it slow, and how a join brings matching rows together.

compare.title: The same report, run eagerly in Kotlin and lazily in Spark

a.label: Kotlin List: every line runs now
a.title: Kotlin List: every line runs now
a.html: val captured = payments.filter { it.status == "CAPTURED" } // runs now: a new list val euros = captured.map { it.copy(amountEur = it.amountCents / 100.0) } // runs now: another list val totals = euros.groupBy { it.merchantId } // runs now: a map of lists .mapValues { (_, ps) -> ps.sumOf { it.amountEur } } // three full intermediate results in memory, every field of every payment carried along

b.label: Spark DataFrame: nothing runs until collect
b.title: Spark DataFrame: nothing runs until collect
b.html: val captured = payments.where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED")) // a plan, no rows read val euros = captured.withColumn("amount_eur", col("amount_cents").divide(100)) // a bigger plan val totals = euros.groupBy("merchant_id").agg(sum("amount_eur")) // a bigger plan totals.collectAsList() // now: optimize, prune to 3 columns, push the filter, run 2 stages

compare.note: The Kotlin version works out each step's full result before the next line runs, and it can't know that only two fields matter in the end. The Spark version builds a description at every line, so Spark sees the whole chain when collect() arrives. That's what lets it read three columns instead of four, push the status filter into the Parquet reader, and do the filter, the arithmetic and the first sums in one pass per task. Kotlin's Sequence sits in between: it also does its steps in one pass, but it runs on one thread and can't rewrite the query.

drill.title: Cut a pipeline into stages
drill.prompt: From memory, write a function that takes the number of input partitions and a list of steps, each either narrow or wide (with a partition count), and returns the number of tasks in each stage. Then use it on: 6 input partitions, filter, groupBy into 10 partitions, filter, join into 10 partitions.

answer.html: sealed interface Step object Narrow : Step data class Wide(val partitions: Int) : Step fun tasksPerStage(inputPartitions: Int, steps: List<Step>): List<Int> { val stages = mutableListOf(inputPartitions) // stage 1: one task per input partition for (step in steps) { if (step is Wide) stages += step.partitions // a shuffle starts a new stage } return stages } // tasksPerStage(6, listOf(Narrow, Wide(10), Narrow, Wide(10))) == [6, 10, 10]: 3 stages, 26 tasks // (a real join reads two inputs, so its first stages come in pairs; this model has one input)

recap: Transformations (where, select, groupBy, join) only build a plan. Actions (collect, count, write) run it, and each action runs the whole plan again.
At the action, the Catalyst optimizer turns the query into parsed, analyzed, optimized and physical plans. That's where filters get pushed into Parquet and unused columns dropped.
The driver plans and hands out tasks; executors run them on slots, one task per slot at a time. There's one task per partition, and extra tasks wait in waves.
Narrow steps chain inside one task. A wide step needs a shuffle (Exchange), which ends a stage: for one input, stages = Exchanges + 1. AQE, on by default, can change the counts.
A failed task is recomputed from its lineage, with up to 4 attempts. Lost shuffle files mean re-running the tasks that wrote them.
The limit: every shuffle writes the rows it moves to disk and fetches them again, and every extra action repeats the whole plan.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why df.count() took 20 minutes when every line that built df took milliseconds, and why the Spark UI shows two stages for it. Explain what happened.
explain.answer: Every line that built df was a transformation, which only adds a step to a plan, so those lines returned at once. count() is an action, so it ran the whole plan: read the files, apply every filter and calculation, then count. That's where the 20 minutes went. Spark split that work into stages at shuffles. Steps like filter and withColumn are narrow: each task handles its own partition, so they chain together in one stage. count() itself adds things up: each task counts its own rows, then the partial counts are shuffled to one final task that adds them. The shuffle ends a stage, because the final step can't start until every partition has been counted. So there was one job, with two stages: the first with one task per input partition and the second with one task. Running count() and then write() would read everything twice, once per action.

deeper.html:
The physical plan's *(1) and *(2) come from whole-stage code generation. The plain way to run a plan is to call one operator's method per row: the scan hands a row to the filter, the filter hands it on, and every handover is a function call. Instead, Spark writes Java source code for the whole chain, compiles it while the job runs with Janino, a small Java compiler, and runs it as one tight loop. The number in brackets is the codegen stage. It usually lines up with a scheduler stage, but it isn't the same thing: one scheduler stage can hold several codegen stages. explain("codegen") prints the generated code if you want to read it.

The scheduler has two parts with names of their own. The DAG scheduler turns a job into stages. It walks the lineage backwards from the last RDD and cuts at every shuffle. It then submits the stages whose parents are done, and a task scheduler hands their tasks to free slots. It prefers an executor that already has the data, the locality from HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived. Run an action again on the same DataFrame, and the DAG scheduler finds the old stage's shuffle files still on disk and marks that stage as skipped; the UI shows it greyed out. That's why two actions on one DataFrame can cost less than you'd expect, while two equal-looking DataFrames built separately don't share anything.
